The GAD-7 is a seven-item questionnaire used as a screening tool for generalized anxiety disorder (GAD) and as a measure for anxiety symptom severity. The GAD-7 began as an anxiety screener for primary care but can be used to measure anxiety symptoms in a variety of individuals including inpatient psychiatric patients (Johnson et al., 2019; Beard & Bjorgvinsson, 2014), infertility patients (Omani-Samani et al., 2018), Veterans (Shepardson et al., 2019), college students (Fu et al., 2020; Byrd-Bredbenner et al., 2020), and the general population (Lowe et al., 2008). Prior psychometric research has shown the GAD-7 to have excellent internal consistency (α=0.92), good test-retest reliability (r=0.83), construct validity, and good sensitivity/specificity when detecting GAD (Spitzer, 2006). The GAD-7 was developed to produce a single score, aligning with a one-factor model, but a two-factor model has also been proposed (Kertz et al., 2012). The one-factor model involves all seven items loading onto a single factor of generalized anxiety, whereas the two-factor model splits anxiety symptoms into two correlated constructs: cognitive-emotional (e.g., nervousness, worry, and fear) and somatic tension (i.e., e.g., restlessness and irritability). Psychometric evidence within a specific population of interest (e.g., college students) represents an important contribution of psychological science to assessment practice. When clinicians and researchers appreciate the reliability and validity of a test score within a specific population, they have a stronger empirical foundation to support the use of a psychological test or questionnaire with an individual from that population. hits.text: DEPRESSION SCREENING IN COLLEGE STUDENTS 5 The Importance of Screening and Early Identification of Depression in College Students In the United States, more than 33.3% of first-year college students reported symptoms that are consistent with a diagnosable mental health disorder, according to the American Psychological Association (Auerbach et al., 2018). Mental health problems among college students have consistently increased over time and it poses a threat to their health and academic performance (Lipson, Lattie, & Eisenberg, 2019). Identification of mental health disorders among college students have been overlooked. Depression is the second most common mental health disorder among college students in the United States (Oswalt et al., 2018). College students are a key population for determining the economic growth and success of the nation. Thus, primary healthcare providers are the front line to early screening and identification of depression amongst college students. Problem Statement The prevalence of depression has risen in the college population in the past decade. There is an estimation of 33.3% of college students exhibiting significant symptoms of depression, generalized anxiety disorder, or suicide ideation (Oswalt et al., 2018). Depression is one of the most common mental health conditions among college students. In the United States, approximately 26% of individuals ages 18 and older live with a diagnosable mental health disorder in a given year (Oswalt et al., 2018). College students with depression can experience a decrease in physical health, negatively impact mental health, hinder relationships, impede academic endeavors, and decrease quality of life (Pedrelli, Nyer, Yeung, Zulauf, & Wilens, 2015).
